chunks.text: 3 Method The preceding sections identify three requirements for reliable cervical cytology classification: spatial contexts provide complementary morphological evidence, the Bethesda categories follow an ordinal continuum, and some cells remain equivocal even under multiscale examination. We therefore formulate the task as multiscale evidential inference, keeping predictions from different spatial views independent until evidence is explicitly combined. Figure 1 : Overview of the proposed framework. Multiscale patches capturing nuclear, cytoplasmic, and neighbourhood context are processed through a shared frozen DINOv2 backbone and independent scale-specific heads. Calibrated predictions are transformed into Dempster–Shafer evidence and fused with reliability discounting to support explicit uncertainty for ambiguity-aware routing. As illustrated in Fig. 1 , each annotated cell is represented using three nucleus-centred patches of 100, 200, and 400 pixels. The 100-pixel crop follows the cell annotation convention provided by RIVA; the 200- and 400-pixel crops were defined by us to progressively incorporate cytoplasmic and neighbourhood context. For CRIC Cervix, where cells are specified by nucleus coordinates, we apply the same multiscale cropping principle around the annotated cell. Thus, the same spatial hierarchy is maintained across both datasets. Each crop is encoded by a shared frozen DINOv2 backbone, followed by an independent prediction head for each scale. The heads are trained using ordinal soft anchors for all eight Bethesda categories, producing a scalar lesion-transition score rather than a conventional eight-class probability vector. These scores are subsequently calibrated and interpreted within a binary benign–lesion evidential frame. Each scale therefore contributes evidence that can support either hypothesis or remain uncommitted.

The three evidential sources are reliability-discounted and fused using Dempster–Shafer theory (DST), producing a belief state that is finally used to route the cell to an appropriate downstream action. 3.1 Multiscale Feature Extraction and Ordinal Prediction For each annotated cell, we extract the three nucleus-centred patches described above. Each view is encoded independently using a shared frozen DINOv2 ViT-B/14 backbone [ 21 ] . DINOv2’s self-supervised pretraining on diverse visual data provides representations of texture, shape, and relational structure, reducing reliance on explicitly engineered cytological measurements such as segmentation-dependent N/C ratio or chromatin grading. The backbone is not finetuned to reduce overfitting to dataset-specific staining and acquisition characteristics, while the subsequent scale-specific heads learn the information associated with each spatial context. A separate MLP prediction head is trained for each scale so that the three views retain independent predictions for subsequent evidential fusion. Standard binary supervision would assign all benign categories the same target and all lesion categories another, discarding the ordered progression between clinically distinct Bethesda categories. We instead retain all eight categories during supervision by assigning each class a scalar soft anchor y c ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] y_{c}\in[0,1] representing its ordinal position along the benign-to-malignancy continuum and keeping the equivocality of ASC-US and ASC-H intact. Each MLP is trained with BCEWithLogitsLoss against its class-specific soft anchor, producing a continuous lesion-transition score whose value reflects the ordinal position of the TBS category rather than a hard benign–lesion label. The anchors are informed by the CIN3+ risk progression described by the ASCCP risk-based framework, but represent ordinal positions rather than raw clinical risk probabilities [ 8 ] .

The binary evidential frame therefore interprets, rather than replaces, the learned ordinal prediction for final benign–lesion routing. In particular, the ASC-US anchor places this definitionally equivocal category between the benign and lesion regions without collapsing it into either, allowing the scalar output to retain graded ordinal information for subsequent evidential fusion. 3.2 Calibrated Predictions and Evidential Fusion The ordinally trained MLP produces, for each spatial scale s s , a scalar logit z s z_{s} . We first convert this output to a lesion probability: p s = σ ⁡ ( z s ) = 1 1 + exp ⁡ ( − z s ) . p_{s}=\sigma(z_{s})=\frac{1}{1+\exp(-z_{s})}. (1) Although the MLP was trained using the eight ordinal targets, the evidential stage operates on the binary hypotheses Θ = { B , L } \Theta=\{B,L\} , where NILM, ENDO, and INFL form the benign group and ASC-US, LSIL, ASC-H, HSIL, and SCC form the lesion group.

This binary frame is used only to express the routing evidence; the ordinal information has already been incorporated into the learned scalar transition score. Because neural networks may produce poorly calibrated, systematically overconfident or underconfident probabilities, and these probabilities directly determine the amount of evidence assigned to each hypothesis, calibration is performed independently for each scale before evidence construction. We evaluate temperature scaling [ 10 ] and 5-fold cross-validated isotonic regression [ 20 , 29 ] , selecting the strategy for each dataset based on validation performance. A scale-specific decision threshold t s t_{s} is then selected on the validation set by maximizing binary macro-F1 over candidate thresholds in [ 0.1 , 0.9 ] [0.1,0.9] . This threshold defines the benign-lesion decision boundary used by the evidential stage. The calibrated probability p s cal p_{s}^{\mathrm{cal}} is next normalized relative to this scale-specific decision boundary. Because the three spatial views may have different operating thresholds, their raw probabilities are not directly comparable as evidence. We therefore map the decision threshold to zero and the two probability endpoints to − 1 -1 and + 1 +1 : p s norm = { p s cal − t s 1 − t s , p s cal ≥ t s , p s cal − t s t s , p s cal < t s . p^{\mathrm{norm}}_{s}=\begin{cases}\dfrac{p_{s}^{\mathrm{cal}}-t_{s}}{1-t_{s}},&p_{s}^{\mathrm{cal}}\geq t_{s},\\[5.0pt] \dfrac{p_{s}^{\mathrm{cal}}-t_{s}}{t_{s}},&p_{s}^{\mathrm{cal}}<t_{s}.\end{cases} (2) Thus, p s norm = 0 p_{s}^{\mathrm{norm}}=0 corresponds to the decision boundary, negative values indicate benign-oriented evidence, and positive values indicate lesion-oriented evidence. Its magnitude measures the prediction’s distance from the boundary on a common scale across spatial views.

We convert this normalized signed distance into an evidence strength: e s = 1 − exp ⁡ ( − λ ​ ( p s norm ) 2 ) , e_{s}=1-\exp\left(-\lambda(p^{\mathrm{norm}}_{s})^{2}\right), (3) where λ \lambda is the evidence-sharpness parameter , controlling how rapidly evidence strength increases as the prediction moves away from the decision boundary. Predictions close to the boundary therefore provide little committed evidence, whereas predictions farther from it provide stronger evidence. The evidence strength is converted into a basic probability assignment (BPA) over the frame of discernment Θ \Theta : m B s \displaystyle m^{s}_{B} = e s 𝟏 [ p norm s ≤ 0 ] , \displaystyle=e_{s}\mathbf{1}[p^{\mathrm{norm}}_{s}\leq 0], m L s \displaystyle m^{s}_{L} = e s 𝟏 [ p norm s > 0 ] , \displaystyle=e_{s}\mathbf{1}[p^{\mathrm{norm}}_{s}>0], (4) m U s \displaystyle m^{s}_{U} = 1 − e s . \displaystyle=1-e_{s}. Here, 𝟏 ​ [ ⋅ ] \mathbf{1}[\cdot] denotes the indicator function. m B s m^{s}_{B} and m L s m^{s}_{L} represent mass assigned to the benign and lesion hypotheses, respectively, while m U s m^{s}_{U} represents uncertainty mass when the evidence is insufficient to commit to either hypothesis. Together, these three quantities form the scale-specific BPA. The three spatial views may have different reliability when their predictions conflict. We therefore estimate a scale reliability factor α s \alpha_{s} from validation accuracy on samples where the scale-specific binary votes disagree, and map these accuracies to [ 0.40 , 1.00 ] [0.40,1.00] : α s = 0.40 + 0.60 ​ acc s conflict − min i ⁡ acc i conflict max i ⁡ acc i conflict − min i ⁡ acc i conflict . \alpha_{s}=0.40+0.60\frac{\operatorname{acc}^{\mathrm{conflict}}_{s}-\min_{i}\operatorname{acc}^{\mathrm{conflict}}_{i}}{\max_{i}\operatorname{acc}^{\mathrm{conflict}}_{i}-\min_{i}\operatorname{acc}^{\mathrm{conflict}}_{i}}.

(5) Reliability discounting reduces the committed evidence of a less reliable source and transfers the residual mass to the uncertainty state: m ~ B s = α s ​ m B s , m ~ L s = α s ​ m L s , m ~ U s = α s ​ m U s + ( 1 − α s ) . \tilde{m}^{s}_{B}=\alpha_{s}m^{s}_{B},\quad\tilde{m}^{s}_{L}=\alpha_{s}m^{s}_{L},\quad\tilde{m}^{s}_{U}=\alpha_{s}m^{s}_{U}+(1-\alpha_{s}). (6) The reliability factors fixed during validation are held constant at test time. Finally, the three discounted BPAs are fused sequentially using Dempster’s rule. For two sources, let 𝐦 ~ 1 \tilde{\mathbf{m}}^{1} and 𝐦 ~ 2 \tilde{\mathbf{m}}^{2} denote any two discounted BPAs. Their conflict mass is K = m ~ B 1 ​ m ~ L 2 + m ~ L 1 ​ m ~ B 2 . K=\tilde{m}^{1}_{B}\tilde{m}^{2}_{L}+\tilde{m}^{1}_{L}\tilde{m}^{2}_{B}. (7) The resulting combined BPA is m B = m ~ B 1 ​ m ~ B 2 + m ~ B 1 ​ m ~ U 2 + m ~ U 1 ​ m ~ B 2 1 − K , m_{B}=\frac{\tilde{m}^{1}_{B}\tilde{m}^{2}_{B}+\tilde{m}^{1}_{B}\tilde{m}^{2}_{U}+\tilde{m}^{1}_{U}\tilde{m}^{2}_{B}}{1-K}, (8) m L = m ~ L 1 ​ m ~ L 2 + m ~ L 1 ​ m ~ U 2 + m ~ U 1 ​ m ~ L 2 1 − K , m_{L}=\frac{\tilde{m}^{1}_{L}\tilde{m}^{2}_{L}+\tilde{m}^{1}_{L}\tilde{m}^{2}_{U}+\tilde{m}^{1}_{U}\tilde{m}^{2}_{L}}{1-K}, (9) m U = m ~ U 1 ​ m ~ U 2 1 − K . m_{U}=\frac{\tilde{m}^{1}_{U}\tilde{m}^{2}_{U}}{1-K}. (10) Here, K K denotes the mass arising from conflicting benign and lesion evidence. For the three spatial scales, this two-source rule is applied twice: the result of combining the first two scales is subsequently combined with the discounted BPA from the third scale. Agreement between sources increases support for the corresponding hypothesis, while conflicting evidence contributes to K K and insufficient evidence remains represented by m U m_{U} . The resulting ( m B , m L , m U ) (m_{B},m_{L},m_{U}) forms the fused BPA used by the routing policy below.

3.3 Evidence-Based Routing The final belief state ( m B , m L , m U ) (m_{B},m_{L},m_{U}) is used together with the three scale-specific votes to determine the routing action. A scale votes benign when p s cal ≤ t s p_{s}^{\mathrm{cal}}\leq t_{s} and lesion otherwise. The routing policy distinguishes confident agreement, high evidential insufficiency, unanimous predictions lacking sufficient evidence, and disagreements that can be resolved by the fused evidence. Table 3 : Five-way evidence-based routing. m U m_{U} denotes the fused uncertainty mass. Category Action Condition Confident Benign Benign sample All 3 votes benign, m U ≤ 0.40 m_{U}\leq 0.40 Confident Lesion Lesion sample All 3 votes lesion, m U ≤ 0.40 m_{U}\leq 0.40 Genuine Uncertain Further review Split vote, m U > 0.50 m_{U}>0.50 Ambiguous (agree) Further review Unanimous vote, m U > 0.40 m_{U}>0.40 Disagree (confident) DST-resolved Split vote, m U ≤ 0.50 m_{U}\leq 0.50 Samples with m U > 0.50 m_{U}>0.50 form the uncertain pool , which is further distinguished by whether the three scale-specific votes agree or disagree. The routing therefore does not treat high m U m_{U} as a third diagnosis; rather, it identifies samples for which the available multiscale evidence does not support a confident single-branch decision. Conversely, when the scale votes disagree but m U m_{U} remains low, the fused belief state provides a principled resolution rather than relying on majority vote. For CRIC Cervix, we additionally apply a dataset-specific NILM vote filter to the uncertain pool to suppress spurious lesion votes. Samples with fewer than two of three lesion votes are reassigned to the benign branch. This adjustment is not part of the core evidential formulation and is discussed in section 8 and the supplementary material. The resulting framework is therefore a fixed evidential formulation rather than a collection of independently tuned components.

The spatial scales and ordinal anchors establish the clinical formulation, with patch sizes dictated by the available annotation conventions, while evidential fusion and routing provide a consistent procedure for combining and interpreting the resulting predictions. Only calibration strategy and scale-specific decision thresholds are selected on validation data to account for dataset-specific differences in acquisition and class distribution. Once selected, all parameters remain fixed for test evaluation. 4 Experiments 4.1 Datasets RIVA. RIVA [ 22 ] is a large-scale conventional Pap smear dataset covering all eight TBS categories, with cell annotations reviewed by up to four cytopathologists. We use train/validation/test split of 10,613, 2,654, and 2,682 annotated cells, respectively. RIVA includes both INFL and ASC-US, providing a challenging benign–lesion boundary, as well as ENDO, a benign class whose morphology can resemble HSIL. CRIC Cervix. CRIC Cervix [ 23 ] contains six TBS categories—NILM, ASC-US, LSIL, ASC-H, HSIL, and SCC—with 8,073, 1,730, and 1,731 annotated cells in the train, validation, and test splits, respectively. Different scanning and staining conditions and a distinct demographic distribution from RIVA provide a cross-dataset test of generalization. NILM constitutes 58.8% of the annotated cells, while ASC-US has only 91 validation and 91 test samples; its results should therefore be interpreted with appropriate caution. Augmentations. Despite heavy class imbalance, no artificial augmentation or class rebalancing was applied. The framework is therefore evaluated under the original screening distributions, where benign cells dominate and ambiguous lesion categories are naturally less frequent. This preserves the native distribution encountered by an uncertainty-aware routing system while avoiding synthetic modification of the fine-grained nuclear and cytoplasmic morphology important for boundary-class discrimination.

4.2 Metrics We use macro-F1 as the primary metric, together with lesion-F1 for the binary benign–lesion task and overall routing accuracy . ROC-AUC and PR-AUC are also reported for the DST-fused output. To assess whether uncertainty distinguishes reliable from unreliable predictions, we report the uncertainty ratio (UR): UR = μ m U ​ ( incorrect ) μ m U ​ ( correct ) . \mathrm{UR}=\frac{\mu_{m_{U}}(\mathrm{incorrect})}{\mu_{m_{U}}(\mathrm{correct})}. (11) Thus, UR > 1 \mathrm{UR}>1 indicates greater mean uncertainty mass for incorrect predictions. We further report performance for high-confidence samples ( m U ≤ 0.40 m_{U}\leq 0.40 ) and the uncertain pool ( m U > 0.50 m_{U}>0.50 ). Silent wrong (SW) denotes the fraction of samples with m U ≤ 0.40 m_{U}\leq 0.40 routed to the incorrect binary branch. 4.3 Implementation Details All scale-specific MLPs are trained independently using AdamW with learning rate 10 − 3 10^{-3} , weight decay 10 − 4 10^{-4} , and CosineAnnealingLR over 20 epochs. Features are extracted using a frozen DINOv2 ViT-B/14 backbone [ 21 ] . The best checkpoint is selected using validation macro-F1 computed from the ordinally supervised predictions. 4.1 Datasets RIVA. As discussed in Section 2 , existing results arise from heterogeneous experimental settings; a detailed comparative study is provided in the supplementary material. Hence, their results provide valuable context but not a controlled baseline for our setting. Our framework targets a different objective: uncertainty-aware benign–lesion triage with an explicit state for insufficient evidence, rather than direct multiclass classification.

A controlled comparison requires fixing the representation, predictions, and task while varying only the fusion strategy, precisely what Table 5 provides by evaluating the same calibrated scale-specific predictions under our DST formulation against established late-fusion alternatives. 5.2 Uncertainty and Clinical Ambiguity Table 6 shows a clear class-dependent pattern in the fused uncertainty. Across RIVA and CRIC Cervix, DST consistently improves over individual scales and alternative fusion strategies, with its strongest advantage occurring under inter-scale conflict. The fused evidence also preserves the ordinal progression of Bethesda categories, while incorrect predictions exhibit substantially higher uncertainty than correct predictions, particularly around ambiguous class boundaries.

These results establish the value of explicitly representing inter-scale conflict and diagnostic ambiguity for more reliable cytology decisions and evidence-based routing. 8 Limitations ENDO routing. ENDO is the clearest failure of the binary benign–lesion routing: RIVA accuracy is 0.222, with 46.7% silent-wrong rate and UR = 0.42 =0.42 , so incorrect predictions carry less uncertainty than correct ones. Its benign morphology can resemble HSIL, exposing a limitation of the binary evidential frame; a richer hypothesis space for such morphological confounds remains an important direction for future work. CRIC uncertain pool. The genuine uncertain pool on CRIC contains only 16 test samples (0.9%), with limited class representation; class-level routing statistics are therefore directional. The CRIC-specific NILM vote filter yields a purer pool, but its threshold must be determined empirically for new datasets.
